summary: For 6–7 year olds (UK KS1 Year 2 'Living things and their habitats'), teach the three-way distinction between living, dead (once alive), and never alive. The load-bearing idea is the middle category: objects made from once-living material (wooden spoon, leather shoe, seashell, dry leaf, wool jumper) were once part of a living thing and so are 'dead / once alive', not 'never alive'. Children sort real or pictured objects into the three groups and justify every placement with observable life-process evidence (grows, feeds, moves by itself, reproduces, senses, breathes) rather than the movement=alive shortcut. Confront directly that a car moves but was never alive, and that a plant is alive even though it stays put.
misconceptions: 'If it moves, it's alive' — sun, fire, cars, rivers, wind judged living.
'Plants aren't alive' — because they don't move about or have faces.
Conflating 'dead' with 'never alive' — treating a rock as 'dead' when it was never alive.
Manufactured items from living material (wood, paper, wool, leather) judged 'never alive'.
'Alive means an animal' — excluding plants, seeds and eggs.
Still or dormant living things (seeds, eggs, a sleeping animal) judged non-living because they aren't moving.

activities.title: Three-way sort of real objects with a life-process reason
steps: Lay out real objects or clear picture cards, for example a potted daffodil, a wooden spoon, a pebble, and a brown leaf that has fallen off a tree.
Sort each object into one of three groups: living now, dead (was once alive), never alive.

For every placement, run a short life-process 'test' aloud — does it grow? feed? make babies/seeds? move by itself? sense? breathe? — and give a reason, e.g. 'the log was a tree so it was alive once' or 'the rock was never part of anything living'.
Include manufactured items made from once-living material (paper, cotton, leather, wool, wood) and trace each back to its source: spoon → plank → tree; jumper → wool → sheep.
Compare a living plant with a plastic plant and a cut/dead flower to decide which is alive, which was once alive, and which never was.
activities.insight: Dead and never-alive differ by material history: a dead object (or one made from once-living material) was part of a living thing, while a never-alive object never had life processes at all. Being alive is judged by life processes and origin, not by whether something moves about.

activities.title: 'Was it ever alive?' origin reveal gallery
steps: Before revealing an answer, predict for each object whether it is living now, was once alive, or was never alive, and say why.
Reveal a short 'was I ever alive?' life-story for each object: chair → tree, wool jumper → sheep, pressed flower → growing flower, pebble → 'never part of a living thing'.
Pair same-origin items so the material history is explicit: living tree → wooden chair; growing flower → pressed dead flower; sheep → wool jumper.
After each reveal, state out loud which of the three groups it belongs in and the life-process or origin reason.
activities.insight: Many everyday manufactured objects carry a life history — their material was once part of a living thing — so they belong in 'dead / once alive', while truly never-alive things like rocks and metal never had that history.

activities.title: Spot the 'it moves so it's alive' trap
steps: Answer: 'Which of these was once alive — a wooden spoon, a plastic fork, or a metal key?' and explain how you decided.
Sort a short mixed set (sun, fire, car, river, tree, seed, egg, sleeping animal) into living / dead / never alive, saying why for each.
Explain why a car moves but is never alive, and why a tree is alive even though it stays put.
Decide whether a dry seed, an egg, or a sleeping animal is living, and say what each could do.
activities.insight: Movement does not decide life. Still or resting living things (a healthy seed, an egg with a chick growing inside, a sleeping animal) are alive; moving or spreading non-living things (cars, rivers, fire) are not.

activities.title: Interview the object (optional role-play)
steps: Ask an object in role: 'Were you ever alive? Where did you come from?' and let it answer about its origin and life processes.
Keep questions tied to origin (e.g. spoon came from a tree) and the life-process test, then classify the object into one of the three groups.
After the role-play, restate the classification and reason without the persona.
activities.insight: Talking through an object's origin story can make the once-alive distinction vivid and engaging for young children while keeping the reasoning grounded in origin and life processes.

checkQuestion: Put out four things: a potted daffodil, a wooden spoon, a pebble, and a brown leaf that has fallen off a tree. Ask: 'Which of these are living right now? Which were alive once but are dead now? And which have never, ever been alive? Point to each one and tell me how you decided.'
checkAnswer: Living now: the daffodil (it grows, needs water and light, makes seeds). Once alive, now dead: the fallen leaf AND the wooden spoon (wood was part of a living tree). Never alive: the pebble. The reasoning must appeal to life processes or to having come from a living thing — not to whether the thing moves.
